newsitem.title: USA: Sector funds offer more risk then rewards.
newsitem.headline: Sector funds offer more risk then rewards.

text.p: During 1993, the Blanchard Precious Metals Fund gained a stunning 100.4 percent, outpacing the Standard & Poor's 500 Index by more than 90 percentage points. That's great news for people who bought the fund's shares at the beginning of that period.
But what about people who read about those big gains and bought the fund's shares at the end of the year? During the next 12 months, they lost 15 percent of their investment.

For some investors, that story sums up sector funds, which are funds that invest in stocks of companies in a particular industry or sector of the economy. But some experts defend the funds, claiming that in the right hands they are excellent tools for increasing long-term returns and even reducing risk.

In fact, you may be able to put sector funds to work in your portfolio. But before you do, be sure you fully understand the risks they can carry -- and how they fit into your overall investment strategy.

Most people who consider investing in sector funds are carried away by the potential returns in such funds. For example, a recent book about sector investing attempts to impress readers with the strategy's potential profits by citing a study that compares three hypothetical investors' results.

The first investor bought a portfolio of stocks that matched the S&P 500 Index and held it for 10 years. His $1,000 grew to $6,000. The second investor was a successful market timer who bought stocks when their prices bottomed and sold them when they peaked. He made all the right moves and his $1,000 grew to $15,000. The third investor bought stocks in individual sectors of the market, choosing the top performing sectors every time. His $1,000 grew to $63,000.
There is only one response to numbers like that: So what?

Fact is, not many of us can choose precisely the right times to invest in stocks, let alone the right times to buy particular sectors of the market. More often, the typical investor will choose the wrong sector at the wrong time -- and his $1,000 might shrink to $500 or even less.

That said, there are times when sector funds can come in handy. For example, say you are an investor who knows something about the technology industry -- enough to make a judgment about its prospects over the next three to five years, or maybe the next decade. You don't know much about picking individual stocks, however.
Your strategy: Make a modest bet on a sector fund that invests in technology companies and hold your shares for several years.

You can choose from several good funds with solid long-term records. They include Invesco Strategic Technology (800-525-8085; $1,000 minimum investment; no-load); T. Rowe Price Science & Technology (800-638-5660; $2,500 minimum; no-load) and Fidelity Select Software & Computer Services (800-544-8888; $2,500 minimum; 3 percent load).

When you choose such a fund, you have a stake in a broad range of technology stocks in a professionally managed portfolio. With luck, the fund manager will make changes in that portfolio as the years go by, dumping companies that lose their touch and adding the emerging stars of the industry. The potential result is a nice boost to your long-term returns.

Some sector funds also can offer a great way to diversify your portfolio. For example, funds that invest in stocks of companies that own timber, oil or other natural resources offer a way to balance a portfolio that includes mostly financial assets such as stocks and bonds.
If interest rates and inflation rise, such natural resource funds will likely perform well -- while both the broad stock and bond markets will suffer declines.

Finally, investors who can afford to take some serious risk might consider buying sector funds that are deeply out of favour due to poor results in a particular industry or segment of the economy. The trick is buying those funds' shares when other investors won't go near the stocks in that industry -- and then holding on when the stocks and the funds rebound.

An example is the Fidelity Select Health Care, which trailed the stock market by 25.1 percentage points in 1992 and 7.6 percentage points in 1993. But investors who bought at the end of the slump gained 98.4 percent during the next three years -- a 25.7 percent annual return.
Almost no one should risk more than 10 percent to 15 percent of their long-term assets in a particular sector fund. Unfortunately, some investors overshoot that mark without knowing it.
The reason is that the supposedly diversified funds in their portfolios might be making their own heavy sector bets on technology, health care or other industries.
The solution is to call the sponsors of your current funds and ask for sector allocations before you buy a sector fund. Otherwise, you might be taking on more risk than you realise.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers mutual funds for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
